# GUI Terminal Samples Reference

How the WinUI 3 and Avalonia terminal samples are built, and what building them taught. The threading contract they follow is in [GUI hosts](../specs/core_session.md#gui-hosts). How to run them is in each sample's README ([WinUI](../../../samples/WinUiTerminal/README.md), [Avalonia](../../../samples/AvaloniaTerminal/README.md)).

## Why the Samples Look This Way

| Decision | Why |
|---|---|
| A real terminal emulator, not a text log | A log cannot be typed into, and it cannot show what a GUI embedder needs to see: full-screen programs, colors, mouse reporting, synchronized output. |
| A WinUI 3 app first | The embedder that motivated the GUI-host work was a WinUI host, and a real dispatcher is what the sample demonstrates. A framework-neutral console sample with a single-threaded context was the alternative; the tests use that instead (`PtyCallerContextTests`). |
| Code-only (no XAML, no `.axaml`) and JIT-only | Everything that drives MiniPty is visible in C#. The samples demonstrate the threading model, not publishing, so NativeAOT is off. The Windows App SDK, Win2D, and Avalonia are dependencies of the samples, not of MiniPty. |
| Immediate-mode drawing (Win2D, Avalonia `DrawingContext`) | A full-screen program repaints every row every frame, and rebuilding XAML `Inlines` per frame is object churn that immediate-mode drawing avoids. |
| One emulator core, [samples/TerminalEmulator](../../../samples/TerminalEmulator), compiled into both samples and the test project as linked sources | The parser, screen buffer, palette, key encoding, mouse reporting, wheel accumulation, paste normalization, selection, and run coordination have no UI dependency. They are tested headlessly on every platform (`TerminalEmulatorTests`, `TerminalRunTests`), and each host adds only drawing, input events, and a map from its key enum onto the framework-neutral `TermKey`. |
| No `Task.Run` | Every MiniPty call runs on the UI thread, which is what the samples exist to show. |

## Checks

`--smoke` runs a one-line command and exits 0 once its output is on screen. CI publishes the WinUI sample and smoke-tests it on the Windows runners, and publishes and smoke-tests the Avalonia sample on every runner: natively on Windows and macOS, under `xvfb-run` on Linux. `--dump <file>` writes the status line and the visible screen as text when the program exits, and the Avalonia sample's `--screenshot <file.png>` renders its window through `RenderTargetBitmap`, which needs no desktop capture and works under Xvfb.

A GUI process reports its result through `Environment.ExitCode`, set before `Window.Close()`; the value survives `Application.Start` returning, which is what makes a GUI sample checkable from a script.

## Lessons Learned

- **A code-only WinUI 3 `Application` needs what `App.xaml` otherwise supplies.** The first version crashed with `0xC000027B` before `OnLaunched`. `Application.Resources` cannot be read in the `Application` constructor (`E_UNEXPECTED`); the generated `InitializeComponent` sets resources through the XAML parser, not through the property, so `XamlControlsResources` is merged in `OnLaunched`. The `Application` must implement `IXamlMetadataProvider`, which the XAML compiler otherwise generates with a fallback to `XamlControlsXamlMetaDataProvider`; without it `new XamlControlsResources()` fails to find `AcrylicBackgroundFillColorDefaultBrush`. And `dotnet publish` of an unpackaged app omits the project's PRI file unless `EnableMsixTooling` is true, which the Windows App SDK templates set even for unpackaged apps: the publish handling for `<AppName>.pri` is imported only then. `dotnet build` output always has the file, so a smoke test of the build output passed while the CI-style publish crashed. An app with `App.xaml` does not notice, because the XAML parser resolves the theme dictionary through the framework's own PRI. The first two were isolated by tracing to a file and by single-variable runs; the same tree published with `EnableMsixTooling` false crashed in 2 of 2 runs and with it true exited 0 in 2 of 2. The sample's `Program.cs` and project file comment each of the three for users.
- **A stowed-exception crash code says nothing by itself, and `Application.UnhandledException` does not see every failure.** An exception thrown from the `Application` constructor propagates out of the `Application.Start` callback and fails fast at the interop boundary without reaching the handler, so the first crash left no crash file. A try/catch around the suspect call, writing to a file, found the real exception in one run. The handler stays, and catches failures from `OnLaunched` on.
- **Test an emulator core headlessly before anyone types into it.** The first headless run found that the first CSI parameter slot was never cleared between sequences, so `ESC[2J` after `ESC[4;1H` arrived as `ESC[42J`: every one-parameter sequence and every 24-bit color was broken while two-parameter sequences such as CUP worked, exactly the kind of defect a quick manual try would have blamed on ConPTY.
- **Keep the emulator core free of UI types, and a second host is one file of drawing and event plumbing.** The WinUI control had grown key, mouse, and clipboard code that was emulator logic in disguise. Moving it into `KeyEncoder`, `MouseReport`, `PasteText`, and `TerminalSelection` behind a framework-neutral key enum made it testable on every platform and left the Avalonia port with drawing, pointer and key events, and a key map.
- **Desktop automation will not type into what it classifies as a terminal.** The tooling refused keyboard input to a process named "Terminal" and could not find the Avalonia window at all, so keyboard and mouse handling are verified by review and the headless tests, rendering by screenshots, `--dump`, and `--screenshot`, and the first interactive keyboard check is a person's.
- **Avalonia 12 differs from 11 exactly where a terminal touches it.** `OnGotFocus` and `OnLostFocus` take `FocusChangedEventArgs`, and clipboard text goes through the `TryGetTextAsync` and `SetTextAsync` extension methods in `Avalonia.Input.Platform` instead of interface members. Nothing else in a `Control.Render` + `FormattedText` + pointer-event terminal changed, and 12 also drops a transitive `Tmds.DBus.Protocol` that NuGet audit flags under 11.3.
- **Avalonia on macOS bypasses the input method for a control that offers no input method client.** With no client, each key becomes text from its key symbol and the `NSTextInputContext` is never called, so Japanese input produced romaji and dead keys never composed. A custom-drawn control answers `TextInputMethodClientRequested` with a `TextInputMethodClient` (the cursor rectangle for the candidate window, and preedit text to draw; a terminal offers no surrounding text). With a client, a key the input method owns arrives as `Key.ImeProcessed` and must be left unhandled, and a handled `KeyDown` still suppresses text.
- **macOS input differs from Windows in two more places.** Option is the layout's third level, so encoding Option+letter as ESC+letter swallowed characters such as `@` on a German layout; Terminal.app and iTerm2 type the character by default, and so does the Avalonia sample. Trackpad wheel events are fractional (Avalonia reports pixels / 50) and arrive dozens per swipe, so rounding each up to a notch scrolled hundreds of lines. The WinUI host had the opposite defect with the same cause: it divided `MouseWheelDelta` by 120 as an integer, so a Windows precision touchpad, whose deltas are smaller than a notch, did not scroll at all. Both now carry the fraction between events (`WheelAccumulator`), and the WinUI host ignores horizontal deltas.
- **Closing a window must mark the run as closing before it disposes the session.** Observe both the exit wait and the output loop before handling disposal exceptions, skip later rendering and status updates, and do not suppress unrelated output failures. `TerminalRunTests` covers the coordination both hosts share.
- **Resize both screen buffers, even the hidden one.** Keep the main cursor anchored to its content while an alternate-screen program changes the grid size, so that returning to the main screen never exposes fewer lines than the grid.
- **Character insertion and deletion must keep wide glyphs whole.** Repair a wide glyph or its blank half split at either boundary of the move, and test intact glyphs too, so the repair does not erase valid text.
